prompt: Audit low voltage RS485 host-controlled same-firmware modules using static local addresses, staged 3-digit slices, broadcast commit, CRC, sequence checks and timeout blanking. Identify stale/hybrid displays and pin/sequencing errors.
review:
# Audit: Host-Controlled RS485 Same-Firmware Module Cluster

**Scope assumed** (stated because it is not specified): one host broadcasts on a shared RS485 bus; N modules run identical firmware with static local addresses (DIP or flash); host transmits a display frame in the form of three sequential single-digit writes ("slices") plus a broadcast commit; frames carry a CRC; receivers check a sequence number; and modules blank their display if no valid update arrives within a timeout. Findings below are conditional on this architecture; where the actual design differs, mark the finding as unverified.

## 1. Stale Display

**Mechanism.** The host writes slices sequentially. A module that missed, dropped, or rejected one slice (CRC/sequence failure, local buffer overflow, address match missed) ends up with a buffer mixing old and new digits. It then accepts the broadcast commit and displays the mixed contents indefinitely, because the timeout resets on every valid commit. The fault is invisible: the module believes it is current.

**Conditions that trigger it.** A slice lost to bus noise or collision; a module rejected a slice on sequence mismatch but accepted the commit; commit arrived between two slices (host bug or retry interleaving); the module's slice buffer is not cleared on timeout expiry or on address mismatch.

**Audit questions.** Is a commit rejected unless all three slices of the current sequence have been received? Is the slice buffer invalidated on any failed check within the frame, not just on timeout? Does the host ever interleave frames to different address groups without an intervening commit/invalidate?

## 2. Hybrid Display

**Mechanism.** A specific form of stale: module M shows, say, slice A from sequence *n* and slice B from sequence *n−1* (or from a different host frame intended for an adjacent address). This occurs when the sequence check is applied per-slice but the buffer is not reset on a sequence jump, or when the commit is accepted on a different sequence criterion than the slices.

**Distinguishing test.** Bump the sequence to force a single-slice loss and observe whether the module shows a mixed number after commit. A correctly designed receiver should either show the full previous frame or blank — never a mix. With same-firmware modules, this is a firmware-level defect, so it manifests on every module simultaneously when provoked; a single affected module instead suggests a local fault (bus stub, opto, RF ingress).

**Likely root causes, ranked.** (1) Sequence not stored per frame but inferred from arrival order; (2) commit validated independently of slice validity; (3) slice index encoded in the same byte range as data and mis-parsed; (4) broadcast commit also accepted by modules whose address stage failed the static-address match.

## 3. Pin and Sequencing Errors

These are design-level audit items; none can be confirmed without schematic and timing data.

- **DE/RE (driver-enable) sequencing.** Host driver enable must be asserted before the first start bit and released only after the stop bit (typically ≥1 character time of guard). If DE is dropped on the last data bit, the final slice or the commit is truncated and silently lost — a classic source of stale displays. Confirm host turnaround guard time and module reply windows; note that **if modules are truly broadcast-only (never transmit), a module with DE tied high would jam the bus whenever its address matched or whenever it acknowledged** — verify DE/RE is tied low on receive-only modules.
- **Static address decoding.** Audit which pins set the address, whether they are continuously sampled or latched at boot, and whether a floating or contaminating input can alias the address at runtime. Same-firmware modules with pin-set addresses are vulnerable to address aliasing under noise if pins are sampled per-message rather than latched.
- **Termination and bias.** Check for exactly two 120 Ω terminators across the trunk and a single fail-safe bias network; missing bias plus idle-high framing can produce spurious bytes that corrupt a slice.
- **Commit framing.** If commit is a broadcast with a distinct address byte, confirm the receiver distinguishes "commit for my group" from "data for my address" without ambiguity, and that the sequence check on commit is against the same sequence as the slices.
- **Timeout blanking.** Verify the blank interval exceeds the worst-case frame-to-frame gap (including host retries) so normal operation doesn't cause flicker; and verify blanking also triggers on *store* of a hybrid frame, not just on time-out. A timeout that is reset by failed frames (CRC errors) is a defect — it can hold a hybrid on screen indefinitely under sustained noise.
- **Broadcast + CRC interaction.** If CRC is computed over slices transmitted as separate messages, any per-slice CRC scheme cannot protect against slice reordering, duplication, or cross-frame mixing; protection exists only at the commit or frame level. Audit which layer carries the CRC.

## 4. Confidence and Limits

The failure modes in §1–2 are generic to staged multi-message updates and are near-certain to be relevant to any design matching the stated architecture; the specific triggers are hypotheses. The §3 items are standard audit checks, not observed faults. I have no access to the firmware, schematic, bus topology, or trace data; every finding should be confirmed against those. Particular unverified assumptions: that modules never transmit; that the timeout resets on commit; that sequence is checked per-slice; and that the CRC covers the frame rather than individual slices.
